turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, it's... to be completely honest, it’s a highly convoluted situation, and my spouse and my primary care doctor both strongly suggested I come in to talk to someone because my stress levels have been just completely through the roof lately. But, frankly, anyone would be stressed if they were dealing with what I am right now. 

I work as a translator and interpreter—I have my master’s degree in applied linguistics, so I deal with highly technical, complex documents where precision is absolutely paramount. It's a job that requires intense attention to detail. But for months now, probably going back to late last autumn, I’ve been seeing this... this very deliberate, recurring pattern in our shared project files. It started small, but now it's just undeniable. 

Certain subcontractors that our agency outsources to, in coordination with this one specific colleague of mine—we've always had a bit of professional friction, but this goes way beyond that—they keep going into the translation memory. I'm not sure if you're familiar with translation memory software, but it's basically a shared database that stores segments of text we've previously translated to ensure consistency. Anyway, they keep going into the system and making these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the text and, more importantly, to the timestamps. They manipulate the metadata so that when the final document is compiled and sent to the client, it looks exactly like my quality control failed. It makes it look like I'm the one who signed off on substandard work or missed glaring errors. 

I’ve documented all of this, obviously, because I'm very thorough, and I took it straight to our IT department. But they just ran some basic, surface-level diagnostic and told me the audit trail is completely clean. Which is just... it's absurd. I know the software, I know exactly what I'm looking at, and I know for an absolute fact that the digital record has been meticulously arranged to put the blame squarely on me. It’s incredibly frustrating because no one is looking at the raw data the way I am, and I'm spending hours every night trying to re-verify my own work just to protect myself from... well, from being framed, essentially.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unyielding belief that colleagues are secretly manipulating software and timestamps to frame them for poor work, even in the face of contradictory evidence from the IT department.

Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the pattern you have observed in the software files, have you had any unusual sensory experiences, such as hearing sounds or voices that others around you do not seem to hear?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know what you're asking, Dr. Smith. You're asking if I'm hallucinating, if I'm hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there. And I want to be absolutely clear about this: my senses are perfectly fine. I don't hear phantom voices whispering in my ear, I don't see things moving out of the corner of my eye. My hearing is excellent, actually. In my line of work, especially when I do consecutive interpreting, you have to have incredibly sharp hearing to pick up on nuances in tone and inflection, sometimes in very noisy environments. So, no, I'm not experiencing anything auditory or visual that isn't grounded in reality. 

What I am experiencing, what I am seeing, is right there on the screen. It's in the code, it's in the metadata. It's not a hallucination, it's a documented, verifiable—well, verifiable if anyone would actually look at the raw data instead of just running a superficial scan—it's a digital reality. It's the discrepancies in the timestamps, the subtle alterations in the translation memory segments... that's what I'm seeing. And that's entirely real, entirely tangible, even if the IT department refuses to acknowledge it. So, no voices, no visions, just a very real, very frustrating professional sabotage.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that they are the victim of 'professional sabotage' involving altered software files, maintaining this conviction even though the IT department refuses to acknowledge it.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies experiencing any hallucinations, such as hearing phantom voices or seeing things that are not there.

turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced any recent changes in your physical health, such as new medical diagnoses, unexplained fatigue, or any difficulties with your memory or concentration outside of this specific work situation?
turns.patient_response:
No, physically I'm... I'm completely fine. I mean, I go for my annual checkups, my blood pressure is normal, my cholesterol is actually better than it was last year because I've been trying to eat more Mediterranean-style meals—lots of olive oil, fish, that sort of thing. I haven't been diagnosed with anything new, no sudden illnesses, no weird aches or pains that I can't explain. 

As for fatigue... well, I am tired, yes, but it's not "unexplained" fatigue. It's entirely explained by the fact that I'm staying up until two or three in the morning, every single night, combing through XML files and cross-referencing translation memory logs. When you're running on four hours of sleep because you have to personally verify every single line of code that gets attached to your name to make sure someone hasn't tampered with the metadata, you're going to be tired. It's a natural physiological response to sleep deprivation and stress, not some mysterious medical condition. 

And my memory and concentration? They're sharper than ever, frankly. They have to be. If my concentration were slipping, I wouldn't have caught the timestamp discrepancies in the first place. I remember perfectly well what I translated on Tuesday afternoon, and when I look at the file on Thursday morning and the timestamp says it was modified at 11:42 PM on Wednesday—when I know for a fact I was logged out and the file was supposedly locked—my memory is exactly what tells me something is wrong. Outside of work, I'm still reading complex literature, I'm still managing the household finances down to the penny. So no, my cognitive functions are completely intact. It's just... it's the situation that's exhausting, not my body failing me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient exhibits persecutory delusions, expressing a fixed belief that someone is secretly tampering with their work files and metadata.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly denies experiencing unexplained fatigue, attributing their tiredness solely to voluntary sleep deprivation.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies any diminished thinking or memory issues, stating their cognitive functions are completely intact and sharper than ever.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient explicitly denies any difficulty concentrating, asserting that their concentration is sharper than ever.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe that anyone outside of your specific workplace or your immediate colleagues is involved in this situation?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I don't think it's some massive, global conspiracy, if that's what you're getting at. It's very localized. It's just... it's strictly contained within the agency and the specific subcontractors we use for these technical manuals. I mean, why would anyone outside of that sphere care about a localized translation memory database for industrial engineering documents? It wouldn't make any sense. 

I've thought about this a lot, obviously. I've mapped out who has access to the servers, who has the administrative privileges to alter the metadata without leaving an obvious footprint, and it all points back to that one colleague I mentioned and the specific external vendors they manage. My spouse, for example, has absolutely nothing to do with this. My friends outside of work, my neighbors... they're completely oblivious. They don't even understand what translation memory software is, let alone how to manipulate an XML tag. 

So, no, I'm not paranoid about the government or... or secret agents or anything ridiculous like that. It's a very specific, professional sabotage orchestrated by people who stand to benefit from making me look incompetent. If I get fired or reassigned because my error rate appears to be skyrocketing, that colleague gets the senior project manager role by default. It's office politics taken to a highly technical, malicious extreme, but it's just office politics. It doesn't go beyond the people who actually have a vested interest in my professional downfall.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, detailed belief that a specific colleague is maliciously manipulating technical databases to sabotage their career, which is indicative of a persecutory delusion.

turns.doctor_question: If an independent, third-party digital forensics expert were to examine your files and conclude that there is absolutely no evidence of tampering, would you be willing to accept that finding as the truth?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I... I hear what you're saying, Dr. Smith, but you have to understand the level of sophistication we're dealing with here. An independent expert? Sure, that sounds great in theory, but I’ve been telling you, I’m here because for months—months—I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It's not a random glitch. It’s certain subcontractors, working in tandem with that one specific colleague, and they keep making these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. They do it specifically so it looks like my quality control failed, so it looks like I'm the one missing the errors or approving faulty segments. 

And the thing about digital forensics experts, even the independent ones, is that they rely on the same basic audit trails that our IT department uses. And I've already been through this with our IT guys. They run their standard diagnostic, they look at the surface-level logs, and they say, "Oh, the audit trail is clean, there's no evidence of unauthorized access." But they aren't looking deep enough! They aren't looking at the way the metadata has been manipulated to cover its own tracks. I know—I know with absolute certainty—that the record has been arranged, meticulously arranged, to put the blame on me. 

So, if a third-party expert comes in and just runs the same superficial checks, looking for obvious malware or blatant hacking, they're going to miss it. They're going to conclude there's no tampering because the tampering was done by someone who knows exactly how the system logs user activity, someone who knows how to make an altered file look completely legitimate to an automated scan. If they concluded there was no tampering, I wouldn't accept it as the truth, no, because I would know they simply didn't dig deep enough into the XML structures to see what I'm seeing every single night. It’s not that I wouldn't want to believe them, it’s just that I know what’s happening, and a clean audit trail is exactly what you'd expect when the sabotage is an inside job by someone with administrative-level understanding of the software.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed, persecutory belief that colleagues are sabotaging their work, explicitly stating they would reject contradictory evidence from an independent expert because they 'know with absolute certainty' that the tampering is happening.
